node.label: David R. Roediger
node.date_label: The Wages of Whiteness (1991) · Colored White (2002) · Working Toward Whiteness (2005)
node.description: A labour historian who studies the historical making of whiteness and its consequences for worker solidarity. His interview explicitly acknowledges Du Bois and relates emancipation to a broader history of labour freedom without claiming race explains all working-class conservatism.

incident_edges.relationship: Relates emancipation and the eight-hour movement to broader struggles over labour freedom.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview credits Du Bois’s general-strike interpretation; no claim that emancipation mechanically caused every later labour development.

incident_edges.relationship: Examines white-worker identity as historically constructed and as a constraint on class solidarity.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview distinguishes historical racialization from natural race and explicitly denies race explains everything about labour conservatism.

incident_edges.relationship: Roediger identifies Black Reconstruction as an intellectual entry point for connecting emancipation with broader labour freedom (acknowledged 2012).
incident_edges.evidence_note: The written union interview directly records Roediger’s acknowledgment, not merely its interviewer’s introduction. It does not explain his whole research programme.

named_group_routes.relationship: Race in the history of white women and gender in the Canadian West: the 'scarcity model' and 'volcano theory' of gender imbalance traced to colonial promoters (1995), and white masculinity, mixed-race relationships and assisted female migration in colonial British Columbia read as the making of whiteness (2001)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. '“Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men”', BC Studies 105/106 (1995), pp. 27–44, read at pp. 27–33 and 42–43: Canadian historians used 'the "scarcity model" (the notion that women's experience improves commensurately with their scarcity) and the "volcano theory" of male sexuality (the assumption of a fixed quantity of male sexual energy)' (p. 27); 'a quarter-century of inquiry into women's history has produced little on the effect of a skewed demography on women's experience' (p. 28); its 'most clear example' is Jan Noel's 'New France: Les femmes favorisées' (p. 29 n. 4); both models 'are based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race. Practitioners of the "scarcity model" never compute aboriginal women (or, for that matter, men) into their arithmetical evaluation' (p. 30); they are 'integral not only to twentieth century scholarship, but also to colonial discourse itself' (p. 31), descending from Wakefield and the colonial promoters (p. 32); white women's experience 'was never determined by gender alone. British Columbia was a class society' (p. 42); 'While gender imbalance increased white women's opportunities for heterosexual contact, it restricted those economic and social possibilities not contained within the heterosexual nexus' (p. 43). On the Edge of Empire (2001) is unread; Orlowski (p. 119) quotes its aim, 'the importance of race to the social experience of gender in nineteenth-century British Columbia' (p. 8), and 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire' (p. 167, quoted p. 120; Carter, p. 119, uses the same phrase). In-period reception, read in full: Carter (2002): 'This book also makes a valuable Canadian contribution to "Whiteness" studies' (p. 117); Rutherdale (2002): 'At the heart of this imagined community was Whiteness' (p. 325), and the reformers' hope that white women were the 'imperial panacea' (p. 4, as quoted p. 326). Critics: Orlowski (2002) holds that she 'fails to invoke what Roediger calls the "wages of whiteness"', leaving 'a binary racial divide that runs through the entire book but did not run through colonial British Columbia', with Chinese labourers set aside (p. 121), and that her claim that 'class relations are central to social relations' receives little attention (p. 121); Carter (p. 119) asks for the North American setting ('This edge of empire had much in common with California'); Rutherdale's 'small quibble' is that the 'Home' and 'Away' relationship 'could be further probed' (p. 326). Distinct from the Van Kirk packet's edges on fur-trade women: this edge is the post-fur-trade settler colony and the critique of the scarcity model.

sources.title: Paul Orlowski, review of Adele Perry, On the Edge of Empire, Left History 8:1 (2002): 119–122.
sources.citation: Paul Orlowski, review of On the Edge of Empire: Gender, Race, and the Making of British Columbia, 1849–1871, by Adele Perry, Left History 8:1 (2002): 119–122. doi:10.25071/1913-9632.5487.

verification.note: Read in full in the Internet Archive capture of the journal PDF (https://web.archive.org/web/20250826032001/https://lh.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/lh/article/download/5487/4682), because the York site serves a browser check; year and DOI from OpenAlex. Byline University of British Columbia. A search-engine summary attributed this review to Greg Dening, whose review of another book ends on p. 119; the PDF shows Orlowski's signature. Passages used: 'the importance of race to the social experience of gender' (Perry, p. 8) (p. 119); 'feminist postcolonial scholars such as Ann Laura Stoler, Robert J. C. Young, and Anne McClintock' (pp. 119–120); 'sharp disjuncture' (Perry, p. 167) (p. 120); 'wages of whiteness', 'binary racial divide', Chinese labourers (Perry, p. 9), 'discourse' never defined, First Nations resistance 'lacking', alliances through mixed-race couples, class 'central to social relations' (Perry, p. 4) given little attention (p. 121); no mention of wage labour for First Nations men; 'a powerful and cogent argument' (p. 122).

sources.citation: Adele Perry, “‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’: Gender Imbalance, Race, Sexuality, and Sociability in Nineteenth-Century British Columbia,” BC Studies 105/106 (1995): 27–44. doi:10.14288/bcs.v0i105/106.969.

verification.note: Journal PDF read (https://ojs.library.ubc.ca/index.php/bcstudies/article/view/969; OJS metadata pp. 27–44; the last page carries illustrations). Read closely at pp. 27–33 and 42–43; pp. 34–41 skimmed. Passages used: the 'scarcity model' and 'volcano theory' (p. 27); 'a quarter-century of inquiry into women's history has produced little' (p. 28); Noel as 'the most clear example' (p. 29 n. 4); 'based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race'; fur-trade historians 'explain their frequency as the product of white women's absence'; Van Kirk's 'brilliant account' (n. 8) and p. 173 (n. 11) (p. 30); 'integral … to colonial discourse itself' (p. 31); Wakefield and the colonial promoters (p. 32); 'never determined by gender alone' (p. 42); 'restricted those economic and social possibilities'; 'my analysis minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'; 'white discourse and white discourse alone'; Van Kirk's 'pioneering work' (p. 43). Acknowledges an SSHRC doctoral fellowship (p. 27 n.).
